title: Keys for Spiritual Maturity and Relational Unity (Ephesians 4)
metaDescription: You can't put a band-aid on a broken relationship. From Ephesians 4, discover three keys to spiritual maturity that lead to real relational unity.
bodyHtml:
Picture someone falling and breaking their arm, and a well-meaning bystander rushing over to help: "Here, let me bring you some healing" — and slapping a band-aid on the break. It would do nothing. The injury is too deep for a surface-level fix.

That is exactly what we often do with broken relationships. We reach for a band-aid: the latest self-help tip, a bit of willpower, a quick apology that never touches the real issue. But many of our relational problems are actually spiritual problems — and spiritual problems are deep problems. As this message from our Grace for You series through Ephesians puts it, it is almost impossible to have real unity without maturity. We live in a world starved for relational unity largely because it is starved for spiritual maturity.

The turning point of Ephesians

Ephesians 4 is the hinge of the whole letter, and the hinge swings on one word: therefore. In chapters 1–3, Paul has hammered home one theme — you are not worthy, but God in His grace loves you, forgives you, and brings you into relationship with Him. Now he pivots from what Jesus has done for us to how we should live because of it.

"I therefore, a prisoner for the Lord, urge you to walk in a manner worthy of the calling to which you have been called, with all humility and gentleness, with patience, bearing with one another in love, eager to maintain the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace" (Ephesians 4:1–3).

"Walk worthy" does not mean earn your way to God. It means: now that you are accepted, loved, and forgiven, live like it. And the very first place Paul applies this is relationships.

Key 1: Let grace change how you handle conflict

Nothing sabotages close relationships like handling conflict poorly. Paul gives two practices to replace "crazy" conflict management with Christ-like conflict management.

Patiently endure instead of putting up or pulling away

To "bear with one another" does not mean excusing or endorsing sin. It means persevering through the pain someone has caused you in order to preserve the relationship. Too often we do the opposite: we either silently put up with people (a miserable, resentful peace) or we pull away far too quickly. There are rare situations where distance is wise and necessary, but that should never be our first, fast response.

Patience begins with being prepared. Paul assumes people will fail you. If you married a person, you married a sinner — not a savior. Patience also means remembering that everyone is in process, and at different stages. Some people will require more patience than others, and that is okay.

Be a persistent peacemaker

Paul says to "make every effort" to keep unity. Not one effort. Not two. Every effort. Echoing Romans 12:18 — "If possible, so far as it depends on you, live peaceably with all" — this is not a question of how difficult the other person is, but of whether you have truly done all you can. Relationships are a two-way street, so not everything depends on you. But have you made every effort? Many of us quit after a few tries and walk away.

Key 2: God empowers and equips every one of us

Grace does not stop at salvation. The same grace that saves you is the grace that gifts you.

"And he gave the apostles, the prophets, the evangelists, the shepherds and teachers, to equip the saints for the work of ministry, for building up the body of Christ, until we all attain to the unity of the faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, to mature manhood" (Ephesians 4:11–13).

The church is a body with many parts and many gifts, and here is the freeing truth: prominence does not equal importance. Some gifts are visible, like a mouth or a heart. Others are hidden, like the pancreas — you never think about it, but you cannot live without it. Whether your gift is up front or behind the scenes, it matters.

Leaders are given to the church not so people will admire them, but to equip the saints for service. So the goal of good teaching is never a consumer who shows up to be fed and goes home unchanged, rating the "meal." The goal is a contributor — someone strengthened by God's Word who then turns to serve others in the church and in the world. As Jesus said, "The Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many" (Mark 10:45). A lack of ministry can actually be a sign of immaturity; serving is a sign of growth. You don't have to be perfect first. Like Isaiah, you simply say, "Here I am, Lord. Send me."

Key 3: Growth is impossible without truth and love together

"...so that we may no longer be children, tossed to and fro by the waves and carried about by every wind of doctrine... Rather, speaking the truth in love, we are to grow up in every way into him who is the head, into Christ" (Ephesians 4:14–15).

Spiritual infants are easily blown around by false teaching, and our information age offers more of it than ever. Beware teaching that says "Jesus plus something" saves you — Scripture is clear that "by grace you have been saved through faith... not a result of works" (Ephesians 2:8–9). Beware "name it and claim it" theology that treats God like a vending machine. And beware the lie that love is simply a license to live however you please.

The antidote is speaking the truth in love. Love without truth is sappy and spineless. Truth without love is harsh — and has driven many people away from the church. Jesus held both perfectly. With the woman caught in sin, He offered grace — "Neither do I condemn you" — and truth — "go, and from now on sin no more" (John 8:11). John 1:14 says He came "full of grace and truth." We see it most clearly at the cross: the truth that our sin deserves death, and the love that He would die in our place.

A takeaway to reflect on

Two honest questions to sit with this week: Where am I in the process of becoming more like Christ? And is there a relationship in my life where there is division that should be unity? The same grace that saves you is the same grace that strengthens you toward maturity and deeper unity with others. You don't have to fix the deep thing with a band-aid.
